title: Adding endings and introductions; the Stardust motif Basie reused
summary: He doctored stocks with intros and endings and developed a motif on Stardust that Randolph says Count Basie later turned into One O'Clock Jump.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Oh, well, when he came back to Chicago -- well, he had practically a repertoire. When we'd go to rehearse for recordings -- no, I would have -- we would have to sit down and I would have to get the endings, sometimes, and the introductions and things like that -- inserts and things

like that to it because we would a stock. Now, I guess you know, like the thing that we did -- Stardust -- that's almost, almost -- we got that together and it's almost ahead after we pointed out what we wanted to do and we used a motivation in that -- da-da-da-da--
"Ok, Old Memory." Well, after awhile and about --
Was that Louie's idea or yours?
"Ok, Old Memory." Well, after we got that together Count Basie come out with One O'clock Jump.
I never put those two together.
Yeah, and that -- well, he just took that motivation and made One O'clock Jump. Do-do-do-do- --
A lot of things that he used to do that I noticed that they were --
Well, Louie was possibly -- it was the most influential musician of the century.
Oh, yes, he was, he really was.
